instance_recommendations.rationale: AMD EPYC-based equivalent of c5.2xlarge with identical vCPU/memory specs. Offers the lowest cost per instance at $0.38/hr — a ~10.4% savings. For compute-bound Celery tasks the AMD variant delivers comparable throughput, making it the best price-performance option for a balanced strategy.

Newer-generation AMD (Zen 3) offering slightly better per-core performance than c5a at nearly the same price. Provides a good balance of modern architecture benefits and cost savings (~10%). A solid alternative if c5a availability is limited.
Current baseline instance type. Well-proven for this workload with known performance characteristics. No cost change; included as a reference point.

Intel Ice Lake generation — same price as c5.2xlarge but with improved per-core IPC. Offers better performance at the same cost, which can indirectly reduce required instance count at peak. Worth considering if workload benefits from single-thread improvements.

rationale.scaling_policy: Steps are aligned to observed queue depth percentiles. The queue is at zero ~27% of the time and p50 is ~321 messages, so the first step (0–50) aggressively scales down by 10 when the queue is nearly empty, and a moderate scale-down of 3 covers the 50–300 range (below median). The 300–1000 range (median to moderate load) adds 5 instances incrementally. The 1000–5000 range covers the bulk of above-average traffic with +15. The 5000–11000 step (+30) targets the approach to p95 (~10,955). The 11000–31000 step (+50) handles the p95-to-p99 surge zone (~31,025). The final unbounded step (+80) handles extreme spikes (max observed ~156K) to rapidly scale toward the max_size of 250. Compared to the current policy, the key improvements are: (1) graduated scale-down instead of a single -100 jump that could terminate the entire fleet, (2) more granular scale-up bands matching actual traffic distribution, and (3) a proper 300s cooldown respecting the drain period.
rationale.strategy_impact: The balanced strategy drove several choices: cooldown is set to 300s (matching the drain period, the binding constraint) rather than an aggressive lower value — this prevents thrashing while still being responsive enough for a queue with p95 near 11K. Scale-down is split into two tiers to avoid over-termination during brief lulls (26.6% zero-depth suggests frequent but short idle periods). Instance type recommendations prioritize the c5a.2xlarge for its ~10% savings with equivalent specs, rather than pushing to cheaper burstable types or more expensive newer generations. The step thresholds avoid over-provisioning by keeping moderate adjustments in the common operating range (300–5000) while reserving aggressive scaling for genuine spikes.
rationale.risk_notes: 1) The current policies use -100 scaling_adjustment which can terminate up to 100 instances at once — this is extremely dangerous and risks service disruption if the queue refills during cooldown. The recommended graduated scale-down mitigates this. 2) The observed max_desired of 161 is well below max_size of 250, which provides adequate headroom. 3) min_desired was observed at 0 but zero_depth_pct is only 26.6%, so scaling to 0 should be avoided; the ASG min_size of 1 provides a safety net. 4) With a 300s cooldown, rapid queue spikes from 0 to 150K+ may take multiple scaling cycles (~15-20 min) to fully address; if latency SLAs are tight during such events, consider reducing cooldown but be aware of drain period constraints. 5) Switching to c5a.2xlarge (AMD) should be tested to confirm application compatibility, particularly for any workloads with x86 micro-architecture dependencies.
